title: Client, Server, and Service Responsibilities
learningObjectives: Explain the key ideas and terminology of client, server, and service responsibilities.
Recognize how the concept is used in real software communication.
Identify common mistakes or risks associated with this topic.
Apply the concept to a small, fictional API scenario.
Review a communication design and justify appropriate choices.

understand.concept: A client initiates a request for a capability or data; a server or service receives the request and performs work. A client may be a browser, mobile app, desktop program, or another service. Servers commonly validate requests, apply permissions, access data, and return results. Roles are logical: one system can act as both client and server in different interactions.
understand.whyItMatters: Separating responsibilities helps place validation, data storage, secrets, and user-interface work in the appropriate component.
understand.analogy: Think of a delivery process with a sender, a message, and a receiver who returns a confirmation or explanation.
understand.analogyLimit: Software communication may involve complex protocols, asynchronous timing, security, and partial failures that this everyday analogy cannot fully capture.

explain.narrative:
A client initiates a request for a capability or data; a server or service receives the request and performs work. A client may be a browser, mobile app, desktop program, or another service. Servers commonly validate requests, apply permissions, access data, and return results. Roles are logical: one system can act as both client and server in different interactions.

Use the protocol and service documentation as the authoritative guide for a real API. Examples here are conceptual and intentionally do not make live network calls.

commonMistakes: Assuming every request succeeds or returns the same shape.
Treating parsing as validation or authentication as authorization.
Ignoring timeout, rate-limit, and failure responses.
Embedding secret credentials in public client code.
Retrying operations without considering duplicate side effects.

guidedTask.title: Guided Practice
guidedTask.instructions: Draw a browser → course API → database flow. Assign responsibilities for rendering, validation, authorization, querying, and storage, and explain why the database should not be directly exposed to the browser.
steps: Draw a browser → course API → database flow. Assign responsibilities for rendering, validation, authorization, querying, and storage, and explain why the database should not be directly exposed to the browser.
Sketch the communication sequence and identify the client/server roles.
Define expected success and failure outcomes.
Choose checks, timeout or retry behavior where appropriate.
Review your design for privacy and safe handling.

independentTask.title: Independent Practice
independentTask.instructions: For a shopping-cart feature, map client, server, and downstream service responsibilities. Include which component calculates authoritative prices and which holds secrets.
requirements: Use a fictional or toy service; do not include live secrets.

hints: Client commonly handles interface and user interaction.
Keep secret credentials out of client code.
Use service boundaries to organize responsibility.
A component can be client in one interaction and server in another.
